transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I’m here because this thing with our kitchen has been going on for almost two years now. I’m sure the contractor, and some people on my block too, have been working together somehow to cheat us and keep it wrong on purpose. My husband keeps showing me receipts and they keep giving excuses, but it doesn’t change what’s happening. The kitchen is still half-wrong, and I don’t think that’s an accident.
Aside from these beliefs about the kitchen situation, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that others around you don't seem to notice?
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t been hearing voices or seeing things like that. It’s more about what’s actually been happening with the kitchen and the people involved.

Aside from this kitchen situation, would you say you generally find it hard to trust people in other areas of your life, and has that been a long-standing pattern for you, even before this kitchen issue started?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I wouldn’t say I’ve always had trouble trusting people. I’ve had normal ups and downs with people, I guess, but this kitchen situation feels different to me. I don’t think of myself as someone who’s suspicious of everyone all the time.
Aside from the kitchen situation, have you noticed any changes in your ability to manage your daily responsibilities, like work, household tasks, or spending time with family and friends?

No, not really. Aside from dealing with the remodel mess, I still do my usual things. I go to church gatherings, my book club, keep up with the house, and we still make family plans. I don’t feel like that part of my life has changed much.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a single, fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief (that the contractor and neighbors are conspiring to sabotage her kitchen remodel) persisting for nearly two years. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech/behavior, and no other psychotic symptoms, ruling out schizophrenia. Functional impairment is absent—she continues to work, socialize, and manage household responsibilities normally, which argues against schizophrenia (which requires functional decline) and is consistent with delusional disorder. She denies a longstanding pervasive pattern of distrust/suspiciousness predating this specific issue, making paranoid personality disorder less likely, as her suspicion is circumscribed to this specific, encapsulated belief system rather than a pervasive trait pattern. The circumscribed nature of the delusion, absence of hallucinations, preserved functioning, and duration >1 month support a diagnosis of Delusional Disorder, persecutory type (F22).
